doctrines/trinity/question: How can the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each be worshipped as God if God is one?
doctrines/trinity/summary: Early Christians inherited Israel's confession that God is one (the Shema) yet prayed to Jesus as Lord and baptised in the name of Father, Son and Spirit. Three centuries of argument — monarchian, Logos, Arian, homoiousian and Nicene answers — produced the creeds of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381): one divine essence (ousia) in three persons (hypostases). The doctrine was then refined (Augustine, Aquinas, Palamas), divided East and West over the Filioque, challenged by Socinians, Unitarians and Oneness Pentecostals, and re-opened in modern debates over social versus classical Trinitarianism, divine simplicity, open theism and process theology.
doctrines/trinity/longText:
The problem is older than the word ‘Trinity’. The first Christians were Jews who recited ‘Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), yet within a generation of the crucifixion they sang hymns to Christ ‘as to a god’ (Pliny, Letter 10.96), applied to Jesus texts that Isaiah applied to YHWH (Philippians 2:10–11; Isaiah 45:23), and baptised ‘in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost’ (Matthew 28:19). The New Testament does not offer a technical formula; it offers a pattern of worship and a set of texts pulling in different directions — ‘I and my Father are one’ (John 10:30) beside ‘my Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28).

The second- and third-century answers fell into three families. Logos theologians (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen) used the Johannine and Stoic-Platonic idea of the Word to describe a Son who is truly divine yet distinct, often in ranked or ‘economic’ terms; Tertullian coined Latin trinitas and the formula one substance, three persons. Monarchians, anxious to protect the single rule (monarchia) of God, either made Jesus a man uniquely empowered by God (dynamic monarchianism: Theodotus, Paul of Samosata) or made Father, Son and Spirit successive modes of the one God (modalism: Noetus, Praxeas, Sabellius). Both were rejected by most bishops, but the Logos tradition left an unresolved question: is the Son ‘second’ God by nature, or only in order?

Arius of Alexandria (c. 318) pressed the subordinationist logic to its conclusion: the Son is the first and greatest creature, ‘there was when he was not’. The Council of Nicaea (325) answered with the non-biblical word homoousios — ‘of the same essence’ as the Father. Far from ending the debate, Nicaea opened sixty years of conflict involving emperors, exiles and rival councils: Homoians (‘like the Father according to the Scriptures’), Heteroousians or Anomoeans (‘unlike in essence’), and Homoiousians (‘like in essence’), the last of whom Athanasius and the Cappadocians eventually won to the Nicene side. Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa distinguished ousia (what God is) from hypostasis (who the Father, Son and Spirit are), and Basil defended the Spirit's equal glory. The Council of Constantinople (381) expanded the creed to confess the Spirit ‘the Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified’. That Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed remains the one creed shared by Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, the Church of the East, Catholics, and most Protestants.

After 381 the paths diverged in emphasis. Augustine's De Trinitate explored analogies in the human mind and spoke of the Spirit as the mutual love of Father and Son, supporting the Western addition that the Spirit proceeds ‘and from the Son’ (Filioque), inserted at Toledo (589) and later adopted at Rome (c. 1014). Photius (867) objected that it confused the persons and was unilaterally added to an ecumenical creed; the Filioque became a standing grievance at the Great Schism (1054) and the failed reunion councils of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439). Medieval scholastics (Aquinas) framed the persons as subsisting relations within an absolutely simple God; Gregory Palamas distinguished God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies.

The Reformation churches confessed the Nicene faith, but the Radical Reformation produced anti-Trinitarians: Michael Servetus was burned at Geneva (1553); the Socinians of Poland issued the Racovian Catechism (1605); Unitarian churches grew in Transylvania (from 1568), England and New England (Channing, 1819). In 1913–16 the Oneness or ‘Jesus' Name’ movement split from early Pentecostalism, teaching one God manifested as Father, Son and Spirit — today a large global movement especially in Latin America, Africa and Asia. All of these stand outside historic Nicene orthodoxy and are described here in their own terms.

The twentieth century saw a ‘Trinitarian revival’ (Barth, Rahner, Zizioulas, Moltmann). Social Trinitarians stress three persons in loving communion as a model for church and society; classical Trinitarians reply that this risks tritheism and recover Nicene and scholastic teaching on divine simplicity. Open theists and process theologians, from different starting points, question classical attributes such as immutability, impassibility and exhaustive foreknowledge. The Trinity therefore remains the shared grammar of most Christians and a live field of debate.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/0/label: How can Father, Son and Spirit each be God if God is one?
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/0/text: Jewish monotheism plus the worship of Jesus and baptism in a threefold name created the problem every later position tries to solve.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/1/label: Deut 6:4 — ‘The LORD our God is one LORD’
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/1/text: The Shema: the bedrock of Jewish and Christian monotheism. Every side claimed to protect it. Isaiah 44:6 and 45:5 reinforce it.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/2/label: Prov 8:22; Col 1:15; John 14:28 — ‘created me’; ‘firstborn’; ‘my Father is greater’
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/2/text: Wisdom ‘created’ (LXX) before the ages, the Son as ‘firstborn of all creation’, and ‘my Father is greater than I’: the core subordinationist proof-texts. Nicenes read them of the incarnate Son or of the Son's eternal origin from the Father.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/3/label: Matt 28:19 — ‘in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost’
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/3/text: The baptismal formula: one ‘name’, three named. Basic to Trinitarian worship; Oneness Pentecostals read the one name as ‘Jesus’ (Acts 2:38).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/4/label: John 1:1–18; Phil 2:6 — ‘the Word was God’; ‘equal with God’
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/4/text: The Logos who was with God and was God became flesh; Christ ‘in the form of God’ receives the name above every name (Phil 2:9–11, echoing Isa 45:23). Main sources for Logos theology and Nicene doctrine.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/5/label: John 15:26 — ‘the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father’
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/5/text: The procession text at the heart of the Filioque dispute, read alongside John 16:14–15 and Galatians 4:6 (‘the Spirit of his Son’).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/6/label: Justin and Irenaeus: the Logos ‘in the second place’; the ‘two hands’ of God
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/6/text: Justin ranks Father, Son and prophetic Spirit; Irenaeus insists the Creator acts directly through his own Word and Wisdom, against Gnostic intermediaries.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/7/text: Theodotus the Cobbler at Rome (c. 190); Paul of Samosata, deposed by the Synod of Antioch (268), which reportedly also rejected ‘homoousios’ in his sense — later an embarrassment for the Nicenes.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/8/text: One God appears successively as Father, Son and Spirit; opponents called it ‘Patripassianism’ (the Father suffered).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/9/text: Against Praxeas coins the Latin vocabulary the West will use for the next millennium.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/10/text: The Son is eternally begotten — there was no time when he was not — yet ranked below the Father. Both Arians and Nicenes later claimed him.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/11/label: Arius: the Son is the first creature
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/11/text: ‘There was when he was not.’ The Son is divine by grace, created before time. After Nicaea, Homoian creeds imposed at Ariminum and Seleucia (359) made the world, in Jerome's words, groan to find itself Arian.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/12/text: About 250–318 bishops, convened by Constantine, confess the Son ‘of the essence of the Father… of one substance (homoousios)’ and anathematise Arian slogans.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/13/label: Athanasius: only God can deify; the Father is eternally Father
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/13/text: Five times exiled, Athanasius argues that a creature cannot unite us to God and that Christians already worship the Son — so he must be true God.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/14/text: Basil of Ancyra's party: anti-Arian but wary of ‘homoousios’ as Sabellian. Later reconciled to Nicaea.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/15/label: Pneumatomachians: the Spirit is not God
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/15/text: Some who accepted the Son's deity denied the Spirit's — the next battle line.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/16/label: Basil, On the Holy Spirit: equal glory in worship
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/16/text: Liturgy shapes doctrine: if the Spirit is glorified ‘with’ the Father and Son, he shares their nature.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/17/text: Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa distinguish common essence from distinct persons marked by unbegottenness, begottenness and procession.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/18/label: Council of Constantinople: the Spirit ‘worshipped and glorified’
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/18/text: Ratifies Nicaea, condemns Eunomians, Pneumatomachians, Apollinarians; produces the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/19/label: Imperial enforcement; Homoian faith survives among Goths and Vandals
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/19/text: Theodosius I enforces Nicene faith (Edict of Thessalonica, 380). Ulfilas' Homoian Christianity spreads to Goths, Vandals and Lombards; Vandal kings persecute Nicene Christians in North Africa (484).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/20/label: Augustine, De Trinitate: the Spirit as mutual love
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/20/text: Psychological analogies (memory, understanding, will; lover, beloved, love) and the Spirit as the bond of Father and Son.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/21/text: As Visigothic Spain converts from Arianism, the creed says the Spirit proceeds from the Father ‘and the Son’ to stress the Son's full deity.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/22/label: Photius: the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/22/text: The Father is the sole cause (aitia) in the Trinity; the Filioque confuses personal properties and was added without an ecumenical council.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/23/label: Great Schism: Filioque among the charges
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/23/text: Rome had sung the Filioque since c. 1014; the mutual excommunications of 1054 cite it among other grievances.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/24/label: Aquinas: persons as subsisting relations in a simple God
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/24/text: Scholastic synthesis: God is pure act, without parts; the persons are distinguished only by relations of origin.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/25/label: Council of Florence: union declared, then rejected
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/25/text: Latins and Greeks agree ‘from the Father through the Son’ may mean the same as ‘and the Son’; the union is repudiated in the East. Modern dialogue continues: Vatican clarification (1995); North American Orthodox–Catholic agreed statement (2003).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/26/text: Servetus burned at Geneva (1553); Racovian Catechism (1605); Transylvanian Unitarian church (1568); Channing's ‘Unitarian Christianity’ (1819).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/27/label: Oneness Pentecostalism: one God, Jesus' name
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/27/text: From the Arroyo Seco camp meeting (1913): Father, Son and Spirit are manifestations of one God, whose name is Jesus.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/28/label: Assemblies of God affirms the Trinity
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/28/text: The Statement of Fundamental Truths forces out about a quarter of ministers, who form Oneness bodies (later the UPCI, 1945).
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/29/text: Whitehead's Process and Reality (1929), Hartshorne, Cobb: God is dipolar, persuasive not coercive, affected by the world.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/30/text: Barth puts the Trinity at the start of dogmatics (1932); Rahner's ‘Rule’: the economic Trinity is the immanent Trinity.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/31/text: Moltmann, Zizioulas, Boff, Plantinga: three persons in loving communion (perichoresis) as the model for church and society.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/32/text: Pinnock et al.: God genuinely responds; the future is partly open, even to God.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/33/label: Classical theism retrieval: simplicity and impassibility
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/33/text: Critics argue social, open and process views abandon the Nicene doctrine of God; a renewed classical theism defends simplicity, immutability and eternal generation.
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/34/label: Today: Nicene faith confessed by most; nontrinitarian minorities
doctrines/trinity/flow/nodes/34/text: Eastern and Oriental Orthodox, the Church of the East, Catholics and nearly all Protestants confess the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. Outside historic Nicene orthodoxy: Oneness Pentecostals (often estimated in the tens of millions), Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians, Iglesia ni Cristo.
